coreConcepts.definition: The fresh, sour quality that gives wine energy and shape.
coreConcepts.whyItMatters: It helps a wine feel lively instead of flat.

coreConcepts.definition: Malic acid is sharp and green-apple-like; lactic acid is softer and rounder.
coreConcepts.whyItMatters: This contrast explains why some wines feel crisp while others feel creamy.

coreConcepts.definition: The process in which yeast changes grape sugar into alcohol and aroma compounds.
coreConcepts.whyItMatters: It shapes both flavour and texture, not only alcohol level.

coreConcepts.definition: Barrel contact and controlled oxygen exposure can add flavour and soften structure.
coreConcepts.whyItMatters: These winemaking choices can change the final style even with the same grape.

coreConcepts.definition: A practical order for noticing acidity, texture, body, aroma, and winemaking clues.
coreConcepts.whyItMatters: It gives learners a repeatable method for understanding a glass of wine.

connectionMap.label: malolactic softening
connectionMap.explanation: When malic acid changes into lactic acid, the wine usually feels less sharp and more rounded.

connectionMap.label: style building
connectionMap.explanation: Climate affects ripeness and acidity, and that changes how light, fresh, or rich the wine feels.

connectionMap.label: winemaking influence
connectionMap.explanation: Yeast activity and fermentation temperature help shape aroma and the mouthfeel of the wine.

miniCaseStudy.scenario: A learner compares two Chardonnays, one from a cool region and one from a warmer region.
miniCaseStudy.analysis: The cooler wine is likely to keep higher acidity and a sharper profile, while the warmer wine may feel fuller and riper. Malolactic conversion or oak aging can make the warmer style feel even softer and creamier.
miniCaseStudy.takeaway: Do not judge a wine only by grape name. Region and winemaking choices change the result.

trackingChecklist.note: Notice whether the wine makes your mouth water quickly.
Decide whether the wine feels sharp, creamy, smooth, or firm.
Ask whether the wine feels light, medium, or full.
Smell before tasting and note fresh, ripe, oak, or yeast clues.
Look for signs of vanilla, toast, softness, or age.
Connect crisp styles with malic acid and softer styles with lactic acid.
Explain how acidity, body, texture, and aroma work together.

Why can the same grape taste different in different wines?

advancedLayer.title: C1 Technical Layer
advancedLayer.summary: Go beyond the learner-friendly overview and look at how acid structure, phenolic extraction, aroma chemistry, oxygen management, and elevage decisions shape the same grape into very different wines.

focusCards.detail: Wine acidity is not just one number. Tartaric acid gives a stable backbone, malic acid adds a sharper green-apple edge, and pH changes how firm or soft that acidity feels in the glass.
focusCards.whyItMatters: Two wines can show similar total acidity but feel very different because pH, alcohol, fruit ripeness, and residual sugar change the final perception.

focusCards.detail: Phenolic compounds come from grape skins, seeds, and sometimes stems. Extraction level depends on ripeness, temperature, cap management, and time on skins.
focusCards.whyItMatters: This is one reason texture can move from fine and chalky to coarse and drying even before oak influence is considered.

focusCards.detail: Yeast metabolism creates esters and other volatile compounds during fermentation. Their expression changes with strain choice, nutrient status, temperature, and later oxygen exposure.
focusCards.whyItMatters: Fruit aroma is not only a grape property. Fermentation conditions can amplify, mute, or redirect what the drinker smells.

focusCards.detail: When wine stays on lees, yeast breakdown products can add creaminess, breadth, and more stable aromatic complexity.
focusCards.whyItMatters: A wine can feel fuller and more layered without becoming obviously oaky, which is important when learners compare stainless-steel and barrel-aged styles.

focusCards.detail: Some winemaking styles protect the wine strongly from oxygen, while others allow controlled oxygen contact through barrel ageing, lees work, or cellar handling.
focusCards.whyItMatters: That choice changes aroma profile, texture, ageing path, and how quickly a wine moves from bright and tense to softer and more developed.

mechanismChains.label: malolactic texture shift
mechanismChains.explanation: The key effect is not only a chemical swap but a sensory shift: the wine usually feels less angular and more integrated on the palate.

mechanismChains.label: fermentation aroma pathway
mechanismChains.explanation: A cooler and more protective fermentation can preserve lifted fruit notes, while warmer or less protected conditions can push the profile toward riper or broader aromas.

mechanismChains.label: structure building pathway
mechanismChains.explanation: Texture is not one isolated sensation. It reflects how grape maturity and extraction choices interact from the first sip to the final aftertaste.

styleComparisons.label: Cool-climate vs warm-climate Chardonnay
styleComparisons.leftNotes: Higher natural acidity, tighter fruit profile, more linear structure, and a greater chance that the wine reads as mineral or saline rather than broad.
styleComparisons.rightNotes: Riper fruit, higher alcohol risk, softer acid impression, and a broader mid-palate that can seem richer even before oak or malolactic influence is added.
styleComparisons.takeaway: Climate does not replace winemaking decisions, but it sets the structural starting point from which those decisions operate.

styleComparisons.label: Stainless-steel ageing vs oak elevage
styleComparisons.leftNotes: Usually aims to preserve primary fruit, cleaner reductive aromatics, and a more direct acid line.
styleComparisons.rightNotes: Can introduce oxygen exchange, spice or toast notes, tannin contribution, and a broader textural frame, especially when paired with lees work.
styleComparisons.takeaway: Oak is not just flavour. It is a structural tool that changes oxygen exposure and mouthfeel as well as aroma.

styleComparisons.label: Short skin contact vs extended extraction
styleComparisons.leftNotes: Lower phenolic pickup, softer tactile grip, and a cleaner fruit-forward style.
styleComparisons.rightNotes: More tannin and structural grip, higher bitterness risk, and greater demand for fruit concentration and balance.
styleComparisons.takeaway: Extraction decisions can sharpen or distort style depending on whether fruit weight is strong enough to carry the structure.

analysisPrompts: If two Chardonnays show similar fruit notes but very different texture, which variables would you test first: malolactic conversion, lees contact, oak elevage, or climate? Why?
How would you distinguish acid-driven freshness from oak-driven roundness in a blind tasting note without reducing the explanation to simple like-or-dislike language?
Why is pH a useful idea for advanced learners even if they are not reading laboratory reports directly?
When a wine feels broad but not sweet, how can alcohol, glycerol, lees work, and acidity together explain that impression?
